docs.title: Minder
docs.text:
A self-hosted home-security appliance. It watches your cameras, answers questions about them in plain language, controls your devices, and — the part most systems skip — tells you when it could not see.

Everything runs on one machine in your house. No footage leaves it unless you deliberately turn that on.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Watches. Frigate detects; Minder decides whether a detection is worth an alert, and sends one with a snapshot and a description of what is actually in frame — not "motion detected", but what the camera is looking at.

Answers. "Is the gate open?" · "Anything at the door today?" · "Was anyone unrecognised at the gate last night?" Asked from Telegram or Discord, answered from your own cameras.

Acts. Lights, switches and pumps through Home Assistant. Standing rules in plain language: "turn on the pump when there is a person at the main door".

Admits what it missed. A camera that was offline between 02:00 and 02:40 is recorded as a gap. So "nobody was there" and "nobody was watching" are different answers, and you are told which one you got.

Recognises, optionally. Face plugins can put a name to people you enrol — and flag anyone they do not recognise. A match only ever adds a name to an alert; it can never silence one.

docs.title: The idea it is built on
docs.text:
A small local model does exactly one job: turn your sentence into a structured plan. It does not act, and it does not call tools in a loop. Deterministic code executes the plan.

"is someone at the front door"
   → router: {kind: query, camera: Front-Door}
   → code:  fetch snapshot → describe → reply

An agent that both decides and acts fails in ways you cannot reproduce. Splitting them means the only thing that varies is the parse — and the parse is measurable. On a 166-case benchmark the router reads intent correctly 90% of the time, on a 3B model running on the appliance itself.

How it works →

docs.title: What it runs on
docs.text:
An Intel N100 mini-PC handles eight cameras. There is no GPU requirement — the vision model runs on CPU deliberately, because on this hardware a GPU thrashes between the detector and the model and destabilises detection, which is the thing the appliance is actually for.

cameras 8 on a reference N100 language model ~2GB, local cloud optional, per-feature, off by default footage leaving the house none unless you enable it

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Walkthrough — six short clips of the portal, recorded against a demo instance
  • Using Minder — install it, connect cameras, talk to it, write rules
  • Faces — what is stored, groups, and proof that deletion worked
  • How it works — containers, the router split, plugins, state
  • Privacy — what is kept, what leaves, and what you can delete

docs.title: How Minder works
docs.text: The technical picture: what runs, what talks to what, and why it is arranged this way. For using Minder, see Using Minder. For the reasoning behind individual decisions, the design/ directory has 21 notes — this page is the map that tells you which one to open.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
Five containers on one host, all on the host network:

Container What it does frigate Camera detection — RTSP in, object detections out over MQTT mosquitto The MQTT bus everything else talks over homeassistant Device control (lights, switches, sensors) — a hidden integration layer minder Everything that is Minder: the swarm, the bots, the webapp frigate-init One-shot: writes Frigate's config from your camera list, then exits

Ollama is a host prerequisite, not a container. The router and vision models run on the host and are reached over localhost:11434 (the stack is on the host network). That is deliberate — it is what keeps camera frames inside the house — but it does mean docker compose up alone is not enough on a fresh machine: qwen2.5:3b and qwen2.5vl:3b must be pulled first.

The minder container supervises four processes:

swarmkit serve /app/workspace --port 8321   # the agent swarm, HTTP on localhost
python3 /app/webapp/app.py                  # onboarding + ops API, port 80
python3 /app/bot.py                         # Telegram adapter
python3 /app/discord_bot.py                 # Discord adapter

Each is restarted independently if it dies. A crashed Telegram bot does not take the cameras with it.

docs.title: The core idea: the model reads, the code does
docs.text:
This is the decision everything else follows from (design/conversation-router.md).

When you send a message, a small local model does exactly one job: turn your sentence into a structured plan — which kind of request is this, which camera, which device, what condition. It does not act. It does not call tools in a loop. It emits a plan and stops.

Deterministic Python then executes that plan.

"is someone at the main door"
   → router: {kind: query, camera: Front-Door}
   → code: fetch snapshot → describe → reply

The reason is reliability. An agent that decides and acts in a loop fails in ways you cannot reproduce: it retries, it hallucinates a camera name, it takes a different path on identical input. Splitting them means the only thing that varies is the parse — and the parse is testable. scripts/router_cases.json pins 166 utterances against expected intents, drawn from this appliance's own camera and device names.

docs.title: The guards
docs.text:
A 3B does not parse well enough on its own. Measured on those 166 cases, qwen2.5:3b gets the intent right 62% of the time — not usable for a system that switches your pump.

So the plan passes through a deterministic correction pass (_correct_plan) before anything acts on it. That takes the same model to 90%, and no guard has ever cost a case that was previously right:

intent correct the model alone 62.2% after the guards 90.4%

The guards are not patches around a bad model — they are what makes a local 3B viable, and so they are the reason Minder needs no cloud for language. Each one restates something an intent already means:

  • A scenario is a standing rule with a future trigger — so "turn on the pump", with no trigger, is a command, not a rule. This one matters beyond accuracy: a scenario is stored, so a misread command silently never runs.
  • A device command must say what to do — so "what smart plugs do I have" is a question, not an instruction to switch one.
  • A message naming a camera is about that camera — the names are Side-Gate, people type "bedroom deck", and matching those is code's job rather than the model's.

They are also specific to the model deployed. Benchmarked against a larger qwen3.5:4b, the same guards helped nothing — that model does not make these mistakes. Change the router model and the guards should be re-measured rather than trusted.

docs.title: Measuring it yourself
docs.text:
docker compose exec minder python /app/scripts/bench_router.py /app/scripts/router_cases.json

Prints per-intent accuracy, what the guards changed, and latency. It asks the model once per case and scores the answer twice — before and after the guards — so the difference between the two numbers is the guards and not sampling noise.

Every routing decision is also recorded to the observation log (router_log.py), with the utterance, the model's intent and the guards' intent. scripts/harvest_router_cases.py turns that traffic into new labelled cases, so the benchmark grows toward what your household actually says rather than what we imagined it would. MINDER_ROUTER_LOG=off disables the recording.

docs.title: The swarm
docs.text:
The workspace holds nine topologies, each a bounded job:

Topology Job minder-router Parse a message into a plan (the hot path) minder-core The general conversational agent minder-device Device control through Home Assistant minder-discover Find cameras on the network minder-doctor Self-diagnosis — the six-hourly health check minder-frigate-config Write Frigate's configuration minder-ha-setup Home Assistant onboarding minder-onboard First-run setup minder-weather Weather lookups

They run on SwarmKit, pinned once as SWARMKIT_VERSION in docker-compose.yml. Minder consumes the released runtime from PyPI — there is no path into a SwarmKit checkout anywhere in this repo.

Tools reach the swarm as six MCP servers (mcp-servers/): camera, vision, detect, tuya, doctor, frigate. Each is a stdio subprocess the runtime governs — every tool call is policy-checked and audited.

docs.title: Vision: two layers, local first
docs.text:
design/two-layer-vision-models.md has the full argument.

  • Layer 1 — per-alert enrichment. Runs on every alert, so it must be cheap: a small local VLM (Ollama, CPU) that says what is in frame.
  • Layer 2 — interactive questions. "What is the person doing?", "is that dangerous?" — a capable model that reads and judges. Local by default, cloud when you enable it.

Vision runs on CPU deliberately. On this hardware the GPU thrashes between the detector and the VLM, and the CPU path is slower per call but does not destabilise detection (design/vision-architecture.md).

Cloud escalation is opt-in per layer (MINDER_DESCRIBE_PROVIDER, MINDER_QUERY_PROVIDER) and falls back to local on failure — a cloud outage degrades quality, never availability.

docs.title: Detection plugins
docs.text:
Optional perception — faces today, cartons on a belt or hard-hats tomorrow — added without a rebuild and without touching the detection path (design/detection-plugins.md).

A plugin is a directory in /data/plugins/ holding a manifest, some code, and a model fetched on install with a checksum. Models are not baked into the image: it is already ~3GB, and one nobody arms is a pure tax.

docs.title: Three levels of "off", and they differ
docs.text:
State Meaning Costs not installed no manifest, no model nothing installed registered, authorable in rules, model not loaded disk armed model resident, running on a cadence CPU

The middle one is the point: you can install something to look at it without paying for it. Nothing loads until you arm it, and MINDER_PLUGINS=off stops all of it regardless.

docs.title: Declared cost is what makes arming safe
docs.text:
Every manifest states what it costs, so Minder can refuse the third heavy plugin with a reason you can act on rather than you discovering it later as Frigate dropping frames:

Face needs 7.5% of a core (750ms every 10s); already armed: Carton counter 3.6%;
budget is 25%. Disarm something or raise MINDER_PLUGIN_CPU_BUDGET.

The budget is continuous cost — 180ms every 5s is 3.6% of a core — because that is what runs out, not peak inference time.

docs.title: Plugins are classified by what they remember
docs.text:
Not by what they detect. Governance follows the kind automatically, so a plugin author cannot skip the consent machinery by not thinking about it.

Kind Keeps Examples Brings with it detector nothing between frames faces-without-names, cartons, PPE nothing identifier templates identifying a person face recognition, ANPR enrolment, consent, retention, provable deletion tracker cross-frame state, no identity loitering, queue length a memory bound

A licence plate identifies a person as surely as a face does — ANPR is an identifier.

docs.title: What a plugin may not do
docs.text:
• It cannot set alert severity. What a plugin returns has no field for it, so a badly-tuned detector cannot wake you at 3am.
  • It cannot suppress an alert. The runner has no route to the alert path at all — a test asserts that on its source. A plugin annotates; Minder's rules decide.

A wrong match therefore costs a wrong name rather than a missed event, and the security behaviour does not depend on any plugin being accurate.

docs.title: Frames: they get what they asked for
docs.text:
Frigate detects on the 352x288 substream — enough to find a person, not to identify one. A plugin that needs resolution declares frame.source: main, and gets one on-demand grab when a detection says there is something worth looking at. Never a second continuous decode: an N100 cannot decode eight main streams, but it can afford one frame on a rare event.

Minder then crops to the box Frigate already found. Measured here: 185x398 out of 2560x1440 — 2% of the pixels at full resolution, and YuNet runs in 9ms instead of 453ms. Cheaper than scanning the frame and sharper than shrinking it.

A plugin that asked for the main stream is never handed a substream frame instead — it would answer confidently on it. A camera whose main stream is unreachable simply cannot serve that plugin, and the plugin list says which cameras it can.

The grab is deleted as soon as the plugins have looked: it is a full-resolution photograph of whoever was at the door, and Frigate's own snapshot is the retained record.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
docker compose exec minder python -c "
import plugin_install as pi; print(pi.install('face-detect'))"

Installing never arms. Reinstalling to repair a corrupt model never changes what is armed.

docs.title: Events and alerts
docs.text:
camera → frigate → MQTT (frigate/events) → minder
   → is this camera armed? is it in quiet hours? does a rule match?
   → describe the frame
   → alert bus (MQTT minder/alerts)
   → telegram / discord adapters

The alert bus is the seam that makes channels pluggable (design/messaging-adapters.md). Minder publishes an alert once; each adapter subscribes and renders it its own way. Adding a channel means adding a subscriber, not touching the detection path. It exists because India blocked Telegram and the product needed a second channel without a rewrite.

docs.title: Scenario Studio
docs.text:
Rules you describe in words — "turn on the pump when there is a person at the main door" — become running automations. Five design notes cover it (design/scenario-studio*.md): count thresholds, zones, cross-camera conditions, quick mode, severity escalation.

The important property: a rule is data, not generated code. You can list, inspect and delete rules, and Minder shows you the rule it wrote before it starts running it.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Where What minder_minder-data volume → /data cameras, events, rules, channel config, monitor state minder_ha-config volume Home Assistant's own configuration minder_frigate-media volume recordings and snapshots backups/ (bind mount) nightly backups, kept on the host workspace/.swarmkit/ audit log, conversations, run state

The compose project name is pinned to minder in docker-compose.yml. Volume names are prefixed with the project name, which compose otherwise infers from the directory — so an unpinned project in a renamed directory silently creates new, empty volumes while the real ones sit untouched on disk. That is a wiped-appliance-shaped failure with a one-line cause; the pin removes it.

docs.title: Operating it
docs.text:
cd ~/minder
docker compose up -d              # start
docker compose logs -f minder     # watch
docker compose restart minder     # restart just the swarm container
  • Minder's SwarmKit server is on 8321, the webapp on 80. Because everything is network_mode: host, anything else on this machine must avoid those ports.
  • Telemetry is off by default. MINDER_OTEL=otlp enables OTLP export to a collector on localhost:4318. It used to default on, and with no collector listening it logged a connection error every ~20 seconds until the real logs were unreadable.
  • The nightly backup writes to backups/. Restore from the web UI.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
docker build -t minder-ci . && docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" -w /app --entrypoint sh minder-ci -c \
  'uv pip install --system -q pytest && python -m pytest -q'

Tests run inside the image because several reference /app paths that only exist in the container. 139 tests; 7 currently fail. Those seven are pre-existing — this suite lived in a repo whose pytest configuration excluded it, so it had never run as a suite until the extraction. CI deselects them by name and re-runs them in a second informational job, so the count is visible and goes down. See the README.

docs.title: Face detection and recognition
docs.text:
Two optional plugins. Together they let Minder say "Alex is at the main door" instead of "person at the main door" — and, more usefully, "someone unrecognised is at the gate".

Neither is installed by default. Neither runs until you arm it.

Plugin What it does Keeps face-detect says a face was visible, and how big nothing face-recognise puts a name to faces of people you enrolled one template per enrolled person

If you only want "was there a face?", install the first and stop there. It stores nothing about anybody.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Three steps, and nothing happens until all three are done.

1. Install the plugins. Models are fetched and checksum-verified at this point, not baked into the image.

docker compose exec minder python -c "
import plugin_install as pi
print(pi.install('face-detect'))
print(pi.install('face-recognise'))"

Installing does not start anything. It costs disk and nothing else.

2. Arm them. This is what loads the models and starts the work.

docker compose exec minder python -c "
import plugins
r = plugins.registry()
for p in ('face-detect', 'face-recognise'):
    ok, why = r.arm(p)
    print(p, '- armed' if ok else '- refused: ' + why)"

If your CPU budget is already spent, this refuses and says by how much rather than quietly overloading the box.

3. Switch plugins on for the appliance. In .env:

MINDER_PLUGINS=on

then docker compose up -d minder. This is the master switch — off by default, because optional perception on a machine whose first job is recording your house should be turned on deliberately.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
docker compose exec minder python -c "
import plugins, plugin_bridge
r = plugins.registry()
print('plugins enabled:', plugin_bridge.ENABLED)
print('armed          :', [m.id for m in r.armed()])
print('cpu budget used:', f'{r.used_core_fraction():.1%}')"

Then enrol someone at Portal → People, and the next time a camera sees a person Minder will try to name them.

docs.title: The rule that matters most
docs.text:
A recognised face never silences an alert. It can change the words — "Alex at the main door" instead of "person at the main door" — but it cannot make an alert quieter, later, or absent.

So if recognition gets it wrong, you get a wrong name, never a missed intruder. Your security does not depend on a face model being right.

That means "don't alert me when it's me" is deliberately not built in. If you want it, you write it as a rule you can see and switch off — not as a hidden side effect of turning recognition on.

docs.title: What is stored, and what is not
docs.text:
For each person you enrol:

Stored Not stored a mathematical template (128 numbers) the photograph — discarded once the template is made their name and group anything about people you did not enrol who enrolled them, and when any record linking one stranger to another sighting

The photograph goes as soon as the template is computed, including when enrolment fails. A template is not a picture and cannot be turned back into one.

Nobody else gets a template — ever. An unrecognised face is recorded as "a face, matched nobody", and nothing about that person is kept.

docs.title: The cost of that, stated plainly
docs.text:
You can ask: "was an unrecognised person at the gate last night?" You cannot ask: "was that the same stranger as Tuesday?"

Answering the second would mean keeping face templates of people who never agreed to it. That is the trade, and it was chosen deliberately.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Everyone you enrol belongs to one group. Rules use the group, not the name — so "anyone who isn't family" keeps working the day a cousin visits.

Group Typically family lives here; any hour is unremarkable household house help, nanny — expected, during known hours service gardener, cleaner, delivery guest temporary — expires, see below (no match) stranger — not a group, the absence of one

You can add your own groups. A stranger needs no enrolment and no consent — it is simply a face that matched nobody, which is why stranger rules work for people who have never been near your house.

Guests expire. A guest needs an end date, and the template is deleted automatically after it. Someone enrolled for a fortnight's visit will not still be recognised two years later.

docs.title: Enrolling someone
docs.text:
Portal → People tab. One person at a time, with a photo where their face is at least 80 pixels across.

Enrolment only works from a signed-in browser session. Minder's own internal components cannot do it, and neither can the chat bot — storing someone's face is a decision a person makes, and the record says who made it.

A photo with two faces in it is refused rather than guessed at.

docs.title: Deleting someone
docs.text:
Portal → People → Delete. Minder then:

  1. removes every template for them;
  2. clears their name from past events — the events stay, only the identification is withdrawn;
  3. records the deletion, with who did it and how many things it touched;
  4. re-checks both stores and shows you the result.

Step 4 is the point. The screen reports what a re-query found, not that a request succeeded.

docs.title: Writing rules
docs.text:
Add to /data/rules.json, or use the Rules tab. Hours are optional — state them only if the rule cares.

Alert if a stranger appears at night

{"condition_type": "face_identity", "condition": "unrecognised person at night",
 "cameras": ["all"], "schedule": "22:00-06:00", "stranger": true, "enabled": true}

Alert if anyone who is not family is here after 10pm

{"condition_type": "face_identity", "condition": "not family, late",
 "cameras": ["all"], "schedule": "22:00-06:00", "group_not": "family", "enabled": true}

Strangers count as "not family" — which is what you want, and would otherwise make the rule useless in the case you wrote it for.

Tell me when the gardener arrives

{"condition_type": "face_identity", "condition": "gardener here",
 "cameras": ["Front-Door"], "identity": "Ramesh", "enabled": true}
Key Matches stranger: true a face that was looked at properly and matched nobody group_not: "family" anyone not in that group, including strangers group: "service" enrolled people in that group identity: "Ramesh" that person schedule always, night, day, or 22:00-06:00. Optional

docs.title: Combining with what Minder can already see
docs.text:
"Alert if a stranger is carrying something" is two things, not one: the face plugin says a face matched nobody, and that triggers the second vision layer with a specific question about what the person is holding.

Worth doing in that order — asking a vision model "is anyone dangerous?" of every frame is vague and expensive; asking "what is this person carrying?" of the rare 2am frame with an unrecognised face is cheap and sharp. The face plugin's job is turning a general question into a rare one.

docs.title: Three answers, not two
docs.text:
Minder says Meaning a name that is who it is unrecognised a face, looked at properly, matching nobody too small to identify a face nobody could have identified

The third is not a stranger, and does not fire stranger rules. Otherwise every distant figure at the end of a driveway would raise "unrecognised person", and you would turn the rule off within a week.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Measured on the reference appliance (Intel N100, 8 cameras):

grabbing a high-resolution frame 1.2–1.5s finding faces in it ~9ms* recognising one ~400ms while armed ~5% of one CPU core

* Because Minder crops to the person Frigate already found: 2% of the pixels, at full resolution — 50x faster than scanning the whole frame, and sharper than shrinking it.

The frame grab dominates, and it only happens when a camera has already detected somebody. Nothing runs continuously.

Your cameras' detection stream is 352x288, where a face is 15–25 pixels — too small to recognise anyone. That is why these plugins pull a full-resolution frame on demand. A camera whose main stream is unreachable cannot serve them, and the plugin list says which.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
Three different "off", and they mean different things:

Effect Disarm stops running; stays installed and configured Uninstall removes the plugin and its model; enrolled people remain MINDER_PLUGINS=off stops all plugins, whatever is armed

To remove the biometric data itself, delete the people — uninstalling the plugin does not, on purpose, so that reinstalling does not silently lose them.

docs.title: Privacy summary
docs.text:
• Runs entirely on your appliance. No face ever leaves the house.
  • Templates exist only for people someone deliberately enrolled.
  • Photographs are discarded; templates cannot be turned back into faces.
  • Deletion is verified, not asserted.
  • A match can add a name to an alert. It can never remove one.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Minder watches your home. That makes what it keeps, and what leaves the house, the most important thing about it — so this page is specific rather than reassuring.

docs.title: What never leaves your house by default
docs.text:
Camera frames. Detection, description and recognition all run on the appliance. The vision model is local. Nothing is uploaded to anybody.

Your recordings. Frigate stores clips and snapshots on the machine's own disk.

Face templates, if you use recognition. They are computed on the appliance and stored there.

Your conversations with it. The language model that reads your messages runs locally too.

docs.title: What can leave, only if you turn it on
docs.text:
Two features are opt-in, off by default, and independent of each other:

Feature Setting What is sent Cloud description of an alert frame MINDER_DESCRIBE_PROVIDER=openrouter that one snapshot Cloud answers to visual questions MINDER_QUERY_PROVIDER=openrouter that one snapshot

Both fall back to the local model if the cloud is unreachable — a cloud outage degrades quality, it never stops the appliance working.

Alerts themselves go out through Telegram or Discord, which is a deliberate choice you make when you connect a channel: the message and its snapshot pass through that provider like any other chat. If that matters to you, both are optional and Minder works without either.

docs.title: Face recognition, if you enable it
docs.text:
Not installed by default and does nothing until you arm it.

A template exists only because someone deliberately enrolled that person, through a signed-in browser session. There is no chat command, no API token, and no automated path that can enrol anybody — the record names the human who did it and when.

Stored Not stored a mathematical template (128 numbers) the photograph — discarded once the template is computed the person's name and group anything at all about people you did not enrol who enrolled them, and when any link between one stranger and another sighting

A template is not a picture and cannot be turned back into one.

docs.title: Strangers
docs.text:
An unrecognised face is recorded as "a face, matched nobody" and nothing about that person is kept. That is why "was an unrecognised person at the gate last night?" can be answered while "was that the same stranger as Tuesday?" cannot — answering the second would mean keeping biometrics of people who never agreed to it.

That trade was chosen deliberately, and it is the difference between a system that recognises the people you invited and one that recognises everybody who walks past.

docs.title: Deleting someone
docs.text:
Deletion removes every template, clears their name from past events — the events remain, only the identification is withdrawn — records what it did, and then re-queries both stores and shows you the result. The screen reports what the check found, not that a request succeeded.

Guests carry an expiry and are deleted automatically. Someone enrolled for a fortnight's visit will not still be recognised two years later because nobody remembered.

docs.title: What the appliance keeps about you
docs.text:
Where Retention clips and snapshots Frigate, local disk 7 days by default the event history a local database until you delete it every message you send it the same database, so misroutes can be found MINDER_ROUTER_LOG=off disables face templates a separate local database until deleted, or a guest expires

Face templates live in their own database rather than alongside events, so "delete everything biometric" is one file rather than a search.

docs.title: Turning things off
docs.text: Effect MINDER_PLUGINS=off all detection plugins stop, whatever is armed MINDER_ROUTER_LOG=off messages are no longer recorded disarm a plugin it stops running, stays installed delete a person templates gone, verified unplug it it is your machine

docs.title: The honest caveats
docs.text:
Alert channels are third parties. Telegram and Discord see the alerts you route through them.

The portal guards all of this. It is reachable on your local network and protected by a password you set at install. If you use face recognition, that password is what stands between someone on your network and your household's biometric data — change it from the default.

Cloud features send a real frame. When enabled, the snapshot going to the provider is an actual picture of whatever triggered the alert.

docs.title: Using Minder
docs.text: Minder watches your cameras, answers questions about what it sees, and controls your smart devices — over Telegram or Discord. This page is everything you need as a user. Nothing here requires reading code.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • A machine that stays on — a mini PC, a NUC, an old laptop. Linux (this is developed on Ubuntu under WSL2 and on bare Ubuntu). 16GB RAM is comfortable; 8GB works if you use cloud vision.
  • Cameras that speak RTSP. Almost all IP cameras do. You will need their username and password.
  • A Telegram or Discord account to talk to it.

Optional but recommended: a Home Assistant-compatible smart device or two, if you want Minder to switch things on and off. Home Assistant itself is installed for you — it is part of the stack.

docs.title: 1. Docker
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER      # so you don't need sudo for docker
newgrp docker                      # or just log out and back in

Check it works: docker run --rm hello-world.

docs.title: 2. Ollama, and two models
docs.text:
Minder's language and vision models run on the host, not in a container — that is what keeps your camera images inside the house.

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

ollama pull qwen2.5:3b       # understands what you ask
ollama pull qwen2.5vl:3b     # looks at camera frames

Roughly 5GB total. They run on CPU; no GPU required.

Use a recent Ollama if you can — 0.32 or newer. Upgrading from 0.21 made Minder's routing more than twice as fast on the same model, and older builds quietly ignore the structured-output format for newer model families, which makes them look broken when they are not.

Skipping this? You can run entirely on cloud AI instead — set OPENROUTER_API_KEY in step 4 and MINDER_DESCRIBE_PROVIDER=openrouter. It is faster and more detailed, but camera snapshots then leave your network.

docs.title: 3. Get Minder
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:delivstat/minder.git ~/minder
cd ~/minder

Keep the directory named minder. Docker names your data after it, so a different name means Minder comes up empty and looks like it lost everything.

docs.title: 4. Configure
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env
nano .env

You can genuinely leave all of it blank on a first run — the web interface auto-detects your network and asks for camera credentials during onboarding. Fill these in only if discovery does not find your cameras:

MINDER_SUBNET=192.168.0    # the first THREE octets of your network, no /24 and no trailing .0
MINDER_CAM_USER=admin      # your cameras' login
MINDER_CAM_PASS=...

MINDER_SUBNET is a prefix, not CIDR: Minder appends .0/24 itself, so 192.168.0 scans 192.168.0.0/24. Run hostname -I and drop the last number to get yours.

Telegram, Home Assistant and cloud AI are all set up later through the web interface — nothing here needs them.

chmod 600 .env                 # it will hold passwords and tokens

docs.title: 5. Start it
docs.text:
docker compose up -d

The first run downloads a few GB and takes 10–20 minutes. Watch it with:

docker compose logs -f minder

It is ready when you see Application startup complete.

docs.title: 6. Set it up
docs.text:
Open the web interface in a browser on the same network:

hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'    # e.g. 192.168.0.42 → open http://192.168.0.42

Use the IP address. You will see http://minder.local in older notes; that only resolves if the host is actually named minder and is running an mDNS responder (avahi-daemon on Linux, Bonjour on macOS). Neither is installed by Minder, so on a fresh box the name will not work and the IP always will. If you want the friendly name:

sudo hostnamectl set-hostname minder
sudo apt install -y avahi-daemon

Then:

  1. Add cameras. Minder scans your network and lists what it finds. Confirm the ones you want and give each a name you would actually say out loud — "Main Door", "Pathway Gate", "Driveway". Those names are what you use when talking to it.
  2. Connect a messaging channel. Telegram or Discord. Scan the QR code, and the bot will message you to confirm.
  3. Connect Home Assistant if you have smart devices. Minder discovers them; you pick which it may control.

That is the whole setup. Everything else is conversation.

docs.title: Keeping it running
docs.text:
docker compose ps                  # what's up
docker compose logs -f minder      # what it's doing
docker compose restart minder      # if something seems stuck
docker compose down                # stop everything (your data is kept)
docker compose up -d               # start again

Minder backs itself up nightly to ~/minder/backups. To update:

cd ~/minder && git pull && docker compose up -d --build

docs.title: Talking to it
docs.text:
Just write normally. Minder works out what you meant.

Ask what it sees

"is someone at the main door" "do you see anyone outside?" "is the gate open?" "is there a car in the driveway" "show me the porch"

It looks at the camera now, describes what is actually in frame, and sends the snapshot.

Control things

"turn off the pressure pump" "switch on the solar heater"

Set up rules — this is the part people underuse:

"turn on the pump when there is a person at the main door" "every night at 9pm turn on the porch light" "switch off the pump when the water level is reached"

Minder writes the rule, shows it back to you, and runs it from then on. You can list and remove rules the same way.

Ask about the house

"what cameras do I have" "what smart devices are connected" "is it raining outside?" "anything at the door today?"

docs.title: If it misunderstands you
docs.text:
It gets the intent right about 9 times in 10 — that is measured, not a guess, across 166 real phrasings (scripts/bench_router.py if you want to run it yourself). The tenth time, three things help:

  • Name the camera. "anything on bedroom deck" is more reliable than "anything out back", because Minder matches your configured camera names exactly. Names it does not know ("the veranda") are where it struggles most.
  • Say what you want done. "turn the pump off" rather than "the pump" — a command without an action reads as a question about your devices.
  • Say when for a rule. "turn on the pump when someone is at the door" creates a standing rule; without a when/if/every, the same words are treated as "do it now".

Every message you send is recorded with what Minder thought you meant, so misreadings can be found and fixed rather than guessed at. Set MINDER_ROUTER_LOG=off if you would rather it did not.

docs.title: Knowing who is who (optional)
docs.text:
Minder can put names to faces — but only for people you deliberately enrol, and only if you install the face plugins. Nothing about faces is stored or computed until you do.

The most useful thing it does needs no enrolment at all: telling you that someone is a stranger. A stranger is a face that matched nobody, so "alert me if an unrecognised face is at the gate after dark" works for people who have never been near your house.

If you also enrol the people who live and work there, alerts can say "Alex at the main door" instead of "person at the main door", and you can write rules about groups — "anyone who is not family, after 10pm".

A recognised face never silences an alert. It changes the words, never whether you are told. So if it misidentifies someone, you get a wrong name — never a missed intruder.

Setup, groups, rules, and how to delete someone: Face detection and recognition.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
When a camera detects something worth telling you about, Minder sends a message with a snapshot and a short description of what it is — not just "motion detected", but what is actually there.

If you get too many alerts, say so: "stop alerting me about cars in the driveway", or set quiet hours. Alerting rules are rules like any other.

If you are missing alerts, check the camera is armed in the web UI. Minder only alerts on cameras you have armed.

docs.title: Snapshots, video and history
docs.text: Every alert is kept. In the web UI you can scroll back through events, view the snapshot or the clip, and mark things as seen. Ask in chat too: "anything at the gate yesterday?"

docs.title: When Minder asks you something
docs.text:
Minder runs a health check every six hours. If it finds a problem it can fix — a camera that dropped off, a service that needs restarting — it asks you first and waits.

It never repairs anything on its own. Reply to approve, or ignore it and nothing happens.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
By default nothing leaves your house. Camera images are analysed by a model running on the appliance itself.

Cloud AI is opt-in and used only when you turn it on — it is better at detailed scene descriptions, and it is what powers one-time training when you teach Minder to recognise something new. When it is off, Minder still works; descriptions are just less detailed.

Your recordings are never uploaded. Snapshots go to a cloud model only if you enabled cloud vision, and only for the specific question being asked.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
What you see What to do Bot does not reply Check the appliance is on — the web interface at its IP should load. "I can't reach that camera" The camera is offline or changed IP. Re-run discovery in the web UI. Alerts stopped Check the camera is still armed, and that quiet hours are not on. Device won't switch Home Assistant may have lost the device. Ask "diagnose" and Minder will check. Everything seems stuck Ask "diagnose". Minder checks itself and reports what is wrong.

If you need to start clean, the web UI has a backup and restore page. Minder backs itself up nightly, so restoring is usually faster than reconfiguring.

docs.title: Where the appliance lives
docs.text: Minder runs from ~/minder on the host, as a set of Docker containers. Day to day you should never need to touch that — but if you want the technical picture, see the architecture guide.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
Six short clips of the web portal, with no narration — each is one tab, doing the thing that tab is for.

Everything on screen is invented

These were recorded against a seeded demo instance, not a working appliance. The cameras (Front-Door, Driveway, Garden, Side-Gate) do not exist, the events never happened, and every still is generated — each one carries a SYNTHETIC DEMO FRAME label in its corner so you never have to wonder whether you are looking at somebody's front door.

That is the trade: the frames look synthetic because they are. A demo of a camera system is a poor reason to publish footage of a real house, and a product that argues for careful handling of other people's faces should not open by putting a household on the internet.

The seeder is scripts/seed_demo.py; the recorder is scripts/record_demo.mjs, and it refuses to run against anything but the seeded instance.

docs.text: Every tab in one pass — start here if you only watch one.

docs.text: Standing rules — what to watch for, on which cameras, between which hours. New ones can be written in plain language; the model parses the sentence into a rule you can then read and edit.

docs.title: People
docs.text:
Face enrolment, and the consent text that goes with it. Worth pausing on: it states what is stored, what is discarded, and that a recognised face never silences an alert.

The clip shows the tab with nobody enrolled — which is the state that matters most, because it is the one where every face is reported as unrecognised.
